subject.title: San Francisco — Proposition F (Changes to Executive Branch Management)

strong: Shall the City amend the Charter to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities between departments, hire deputy mayors, and hire some and fire most department heads; and to allow City officials to remove members of boards and commissions without cause?

text: This measure requires 50%+1 affirmative votes to pass.
How “F” Got on the Ballot

On July 23, 2026, the Department of Elections certified that the initiative petition calling for Proposition F to be placed on the ballot had a sufficient number of valid signatures to qualify the measure for the ballot.

53,076 signatures were required to place an initiative Charter Amendment on the ballot. This number is equal to 10% of the registered voters at the time a “Notice of Intent to Circulate Petition” was published. A random check of the signatures submitted by the proponents of the initiative petition prior to the July 6, 2026, submission deadline showed that the total number of valid signatures was greater than the number required.

The Mayor is the chief executive officer of the City. The Mayor directly supervises nearly 50 City departments, which are established by Charter or ordinance. Most City departments are established by Charter.

Transfer of Functions: The Mayor can transfer responsibilities between departments established by ordinance, as long as the Board of Supervisors (Board) does not object. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities for departments established by the Charter.
Deputy Mayors: The Mayor cannot hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.

Department Heads: In most cases, the Mayor must select a department head from candidates recommended by the board or commission that oversees that department. Usually, the board or commission can fire the department head, but the Mayor cannot.

Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials appoint members to City boards and commissions. Appointed members can usually only be suspended or removed if the member engaged in official misconduct or committed certain felonies.
Proposition F would amend the Charter to allow the Mayor to do the following:

Transfer of Functions: Transfer responsibilities between most departments or combine departments under a single department head, regardless of whether the Department was established by ordinance or Charter and as long as the Board does not object. The Mayor cannot eliminate any responsibilities established by Charter. The Mayor could also assign the oversight of these transferred responsibilities to that department’s commission. The Mayor cannot transfer responsibilities of these departments:

City Administrator, Controller, Board of Appeals, Port, Airport, Asian Art Museum, Fine Arts Museums, San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency, Public Utilities Commission, Civil Service Commission, Department of Human Resources, Retirement Board, Health Service System, Department of Elections, Ethics Commission, or departments headed by other elected officials.

The responsibilities of the Department of Police Accountability cannot be transferred to the Police Department, and the responsibilities of the Sheriff’s Inspector General cannot be transferred to the Sheriff.
Deputy Mayors: Hire deputy mayors to supervise most departments established by the Charter.
Department Heads: Hire some and fire most department heads without board or commission involvement. The Mayor cannot hire or fire certain department heads that are exempt (see
in Words You Need To Know).

Commissioners: In addition to the Mayor, the Board and other officials who appoint board and commission members could remove them at any time without cause. This does not apply to the Board of Appeals, Civil Service Commission, or Ethics Commission. The Mayor cannot eliminate any board or commission established by the Charter.

If you vote “yes,” you want to expand the Mayor’s authority to transfer responsibilities, hire deputy mayors, hire some and fire most department heads, and allow City officials to remove members of boards or commissions without cause.
If you vote “no,” you do not want to make these changes.
City Controller Greg Wagner has issued the following statement on the fiscal impact of Proposition F:
Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would have a minimal impact on the cost of government, although at a level that cannot be determined at this time.

The proposed Charter amendment would (1) expand the Mayor’s authority to hire and remove most departments heads; (2) allow most commissioners to be removed at will by their appointing authority; (3) authorize the Mayor to reorganize departments and adjust reporting relationships within the executive branch, subject to potential rejection by the Board of Supervisors; and (4) allow the use of deputy mayors.

The proposed Charter amendment authorizes the Mayor to utilize deputy mayors. The average annual cost for a deputy mayor would be approximately $250,000. The proposed Charter amendment allows the Mayor to restructure departments and reorient reporting relationships within the executive branch. The potential costs or savings incurred for such changes cannot be determined without knowing which departments would be involved and how the departments would be restructured. For example, in Fiscal Year 2022-23 when the Department of Sanitation and Streets merged into the Department of Public Works, the Controller’s Office estimated cost savings of $3.5 million in the first year and $2.5 million in the second year of the merger. Cost savings came from removing duplicative administrative and information technology staff, departmental leadership, and one-time and ongoing costs, such as equipment and professional services.

Over decades, San Francisco’s governing system - or city charter - has increasingly grown to reward city insiders. Mayor Lurie is leading a citywide coalition to make the system more accountable to everyday San Franciscans.
Clean Up City Hall is a package of Props A, D, E and F to improve neighborhood services, speed up permitting and reduce wasteful spending so we can invest in our great city.

strong: PROP F TACKLES CITY HALL CORRUPTION.

text: The current system allows departments to operate as independent fiefdoms instead of coordinated parts of government. It protects the insiders instead of holding them accountable. Six department heads have been indicted or investigated for corruption in the last decade. The mayor can only hire and remove a handful of department heads when self-dealing is exposed or they fail to do their job.
Allowing the mayor to hire and remove most of their department heads will ensure city officials are accountable to the public.
Better organized and more accountable departments will deliver faster permits, cleaner streets and projects done on time and on budget.

“Departments that act as their own kingdoms are where corruption can grow. F makes it clear that every department head is ultimately accountable to the people of San Francisco” - Louise Renne, former San Francisco City Attorney & CA Deputy Attorney General

The Board of Supervisors will still have oversight over city departments and a majority of the Board can reject any changes the mayor makes. Watchdog commissions like Ethics and police oversight remain fully independent.
San Francisco works best when we work in coalitions together. Please join the citywide coalition to make the system accountable to all!

arguments.title: PROP F CAME FROM AN OPEN, COLLABORATIVE

text: Mayor Lurie and Board President Mandelman convened San Francisco’s first citywide Charter Reform Working Group in decades, followed by dozens of stakeholder meetings and labor negotiations leading to real compromise. The City Controller has completed a full cost analysis, and the citywide coalition of people across the political spectrum backing these common sense reforms is broad and growing.

Watchdog agencies like ethics and police oversight remain fully independent. No department functions can be eliminated without a vote of the people. The executive branch can only combine services where costly overlaps slow down city services, like Planning and DBI.
The system allows departments to operate as independent fiefdoms. Department heads have been indicted, and when self dealing is exposed, the mayor can’t easily remove them.

Commission seats have long been handed out as rewards, with no accountability to voters. F doesn’t eliminate a single commission, but lets the Mayor and Board remove commissioners who don’t show up, don’t do the work, or are corrupt.

F isn’t about one person. It’s about making government work for everyday people, no matter who holds office. The insiders are misleading because they are being challenged. They think the system works great. San Franciscans know the system is broken.
It’s time for a change.

arguments.title: Clear Accountability for City Government

text:
San Francisco’s Mayor is the city’s chief executive but today directly appoints and removes only 6% of department heads. Responsibility is scattered across dozens of commissions and overlapping approval processes, making it nearly impossible for voters
to know who is accountable when city government succeeds or fails.

This measure is drawn directly from SPUR’s 2026 Charter for Change report and its 2024 Designed to Serve research — the product of SPUR’s decades of nonpartisan work studying how San Francisco’s city government actually functions, and how it can work better.

The measure gives the Mayor authority to appoint and remove most department heads, while preserving Board approval for the Controller, City Administrator, and Human Resources Director. It allows the Mayor to organize their office effectively, including using deputy mayors — a basic tool most big-city mayors already have. And it lets the Mayor propose reorganizing departments, subject to Board rejection within 60 days, so the government can adapt without a citywide election every time.

Critically, independent oversight is protected: the Ethics Commission, Elections Commission, Controller, City Administrator, Board of Appeals, Civil Service Commission, and elected officials like the City Attorney and District Attorney are all exempted.
When authority and accountability are aligned, voters can judge elected officials’ performance at the ballot box. This measure ends the finger-pointing.

text: GOOD GOVERNANCE LEADERS AGREE PROP F WILL IMPROVE ACCOUNTABILITY.

We’ve worked inside San Francisco’s government, and we’ve seen the problem firsthand: departments that operate like independent fiefdoms instead of coordinated parts of one city government. When no one is clearly accountable, no one is truly responsible — and corruption grows in the gaps. Prop F fixes this broken system by letting the mayor hire and remove their own department heads, so corrupt or ineffective insiders answer to democratically elected leadership.

Importantly, Prop F doesn’t concentrate power without checks. The Board of Supervisors can reject any reorganization proposed by the mayor. Independent watchdog commissions — Ethics, Elections, police oversight — stay exactly as independent as they are today. This is the kind of structural reform that good governance requires: clear lines of accountability, paired with real checks and balances. Vote Yes on Prop F for stronger accountability and better city services.

Former Deputy City Attorney James Lazarus

text: LABOR GROUPS SAY YES ON F FOR MORE ACCOUNTABILITY.

Working people show up and do the job every day — city government should be held to the same standard. Instead, San Francisco’s departments too often fall short, yet never face real accountability. When departments fail without consequence, it’s frontline workers and the public who pay the price through delayed projects, wasted public dollars, and services that don’t work.

Prop F forces corrupt and ineffective department leadership to answer to democratically elected officials, not more city hall insiders. Accountable government means better-run departments, faster project delivery, and public dollars spent on real results instead of protecting insiders. Labor stands for accountability at every level: Vote Yes on Prop F for more responsible city government.

text: SMALL AND BIG BUSINESSES URGE BETTER RESULTS THROUGH PROP F.

San Francisco’s businesses know the frustration of dealing with a city government where departments act in silos with confusing and conflicting rules instead of as one coordinated city government. The lack of coordination and accountability costs businesses time and money, as permits stall and project costs balloon.

Prop F creates clear reporting lines, so leadership is accountable to voters instead of hidden from them. Accountable city government means faster permits, better-run departments, and a city that works better for the businesses trying to build, hire, and grow here. San Francisco’s business community supports real accountability: Vote Yes on Prop F.

text: CHINATOWN LEADERS URGE YES ON F TO END GOVERNMENT EXCUSES.

For too long, Chinatown and immigrant communities have dealt with a City Hall where government services fall short. Departments act in silos instead of coordinating and when something goes wrong, our community services suffer. Currently, the mayor cannot remove most department heads. That means the people responsible for delivering city services to Chinatown often face no consequences when they fail.

Prob F will ensure a more accountable city government with faster, better-run services for every neighborhood. Chinatown deserves a government that answers for its results without excuses. Vote Yes on Prop F for stronger accountability.

arguments.title: Street Safety Advocates Say No on F! Don’t Let Politics Block Lifesaving Progress

text: Since 2014, over 350 people have been killed in crashes on San Francisco’s streets. A woman hit by a truck on Market Street on August 7 marked the seventeenth tragic death this year alone.

We can fix our streets and save lives. Through the SFMTA’s Quick Build program, improvements like new lighting, new traffic signals, new crosswalks, and road diets have kept traffic flowing while making city streets safer.
Prop F politicizes the SFMTA Board, which must approve street projects. With Prop F, a mayor could remove a board member without cause — for any reason.

Special interests who oppose street safety improvements can and will exploit this. One phone call to the mayor’s office could halt lifesaving fixes on our streets. Even a mayor who wants to promote safety will be under pressure to fold.

As neighborhood advocates, we know San Franciscans want safer streets. When done thoughtfully, street projects enjoy widespread support in our communities. But we’ve also seen unrepresentative opposition, from a connected few, block improvements most neighbors want.

Voters have already rejected political meddling in our streets. Approved in a landslide, 1999’s Prop E deliberately structured the SFMTA Board to be independent of City Hall bickering. Prop F reneges on that deal.
We cannot afford to go back to letting politics block lifesaving improvements on our streets.
